loci.name: bssa14-single-vs30-kathmandu-basin
loci.one_line: Is BSSA14 with one Vs30 adequate for Nepal scenarios, or must the Atlas add Himalaya-specific GMPE choice and a Vs30/basin-amplification layer (Kathmandu valley), validated against Gorkha 2015 records?
loci.rationale: Contradiction cluster rock-gmpe-vs-basin. METEOR (hazard-map PGA grid) supports a generic first-order approach; EEFIT Kathmandu site-amplification note and the two Gorkha strong-motion/attenuation notes show Himalaya-specific relations fit better and basin amplification (~0.4 s, ~5 s) exceeds code spectra. Corpus is abstract-only for two of them and does not say which open Vs30 proxy (USGS slope-based, geology-based) or GMPE logic tree is practical in a static JS site.

opposing_positions.position: Generic NGA-West2 (BSSA14) with Vs30 scaling gives defensible first-order PGA bands for a public scenario tool
Gorkha records favour Himalaya-specific relations and show basin amplification that rock-only PGA misses

suggested_searches: Gorkha 2015 GMPE evaluation BSSA14 residuals Nepal
Vs30 map Nepal Kathmandu valley slope proxy
Kathmandu basin amplification PGA Gorkha USGS ShakeMap comparison
ground motion model selection Himalaya subduction GMPE Nepal

loci.name: constant-celerity-routing-vs-process-chain-glof
loci.one_line: How wrong is a triangular/rectangular hydrograph at three constant wave speeds against observed GLOF/debris-flow events (Palcacocha, Melamchi 2021, Thame 2024, Tsho Rolpa), and what minimal upgrade (attenuation, slope-dependent celerity, uncertainty bounds, honest labelling) is justified?
loci.rationale: Cluster simple-routing-vs-process-chain. Mergili 2020 back-calculation gives 36-70 min travel bounds usable by simple routing; Hoch 2019 (model complexity), the Melamchi erosional-cascade preprint, Kayastha & Maskey Tsho Rolpa NWS-BREACH peaks, and the Thame EGU abstract argue entrainment/sediment cascades make constant-celerity routing misleading. The corpus gestures at but does not quantify error vs observed arrival times.

opposing_positions.position: Simple celerity/kinematic routing is transparent, fast and gives usable travel-time bounds
Sediment-laden cascades and model complexity change arrival time and peak enough that constant-speed routing misleads

suggested_searches: GLOF flood wave celerity empirical travel time Himalaya Dig Tsho Chorabari
Thame 2024 GLOF arrival time Bhote Koshi 2026 observed travel time
Melamchi 2021 flood hydrograph peak discharge travel time
HEC-RAS vs kinematic GLOF routing uncertainty public hazard map
Manning-based celerity debris flood GLOF scenario simple model validation

loci.name: glof-origin-selection-beyond-pdgl-list
loci.one_line: Should the Atlas offer GLOF scenario origins beyond the 21 ICIMOD PDGLs (small lakes, cascades, Tibet-side lakes, 2024 Thame and 2026 Bhotekoshi events), and what open lake inventories and dam/volume data would support it responsibly?
loci.rationale: Cluster pdgl-list-vs-small-lakes. ICIMOD 2020 inventory (3,624 lakes, 21 PDGLs) versus the Cook et al. EGU25 abstract showing Thame came from two small lakes not on any danger list, plus the Al Jazeera and Nepal Economic Forum pieces. Corpus does not say what inventories (GLAKES, Kashmir/Tibet, Cook/Quincey) and volume-area scaling are open and usable, nor the responsibility risk of publishing scenarios for lakes with no assessment.

opposing_positions.position: The ICIMOD PDGL list is the authoritative, criteria-based basis for GLOF scenario origins
Thame 2024 and the 2026 transboundary event show the list misses cascade, small-lake and upstream-Tibet hazards

suggested_searches: Thame 2024 GLOF Cook Brun cascade small lakes not dangerous
GLOF susceptibility ranking Nepal Tibet lakes open dataset 2024
volume-area scaling glacial lake open inventory GLAKES Nepal
how scenario-based GLOF hazard maps communicated without site assessment ethics

loci.name: scenario-uncertainty-communication-and-framing
loci.one_line: How should scenario maps and printable reports show uncertainty, avoid crisp safe/unsafe lines and frame scenarios as hypothetical, in plain Nepali and English?
loci.rationale: Cluster probability-formats: Demichelis & Ongaro 2024, Lindell 2020 hazard-map comprehension, Haughton & White 2018 on contestation, and the DHM bulletin analysis (gc-communicating-complex-forecasts) point at the issue and Mongabay 2026 shows generic Nepali-only messages failing; none gives tested guidance for Nepali-language scenario tools or for misreading scenarios as live warnings.
suggested_searches: hazard map comprehension experiment uncertainty ranges vs single value
scenario vs forecast confusion public risk communication disclaimer
Nepali language risk communication evaluation flood maps
USGS ShakeMap PAGER uncertainty communication evaluation

loci.name: atlas-role-in-warning-ecosystem
loci.one_line: What can a static, unofficial site add to Nepal warning dissemination (CAP feeds, BIPAD/WMO SWIC alignment, partnerships) without competing with official channels, and how is it kept current and funded?
loci.rationale: Reducing-flood-casualties note and Ncell SMS note report deaths falling 166 to 27 and 4.4M alerts; Sixteen-minutes and Missing-on-early-warning notes show accurate alerts still yielding ~250 deaths, Nepali-only generic SMS and 5h-late posts. Corpus does not say where a read-only atlas fits (lead time, scenario vs live, disclaimers, Nepali-first alerts).

opposing_positions.position: Forecasting/SMS system has succeeded; fatalities fell
Dissemination still fails for flash floods, GLOFs and transboundary events

suggested_searches: Nepal early warning last mile evaluation 2024 floods
community-based early warning Nepal evaluation digital tools
transboundary flood alert Nepal China India data sharing

loci.name: reach-offline-lowbandwidth-bilingual
loci.one_line: Who can actually use the Atlas: how do conflicting connectivity estimates, language/literacy and accessibility evidence change priorities (offline PWA, PMTiles, SMS/print, voice, Nepali-first, a11y)?
loci.rationale: Batch9 gives MICS 82% household internet vs ITU 48.4% individual use; Karnali 68.5%. Offline PMTiles and accessibility checklist notes hint at solutions but not Nepal-specific evidence of which delivery mode wins for at-risk, low-literacy groups.

opposing_positions.position: Connectivity is high (82% households), web-first is fine
Individual use ~48-56%; large offline/low-bandwidth minority, so web-only misses at-risk users

suggested_searches: Nepal MICS 2024 internet households
Nepal digital literacy disaster information rural Karnali
PWA offline disaster map low bandwidth evaluation
